title: Treacle tart
subtitle: classic British golden syrup tart with a breadcrumb filling
excerpt: Treacle tart is a shortcrust pastry case filled with golden syrup thickened by white breadcrumbs and sharpened with lemon juice. You get a filling that sets to a soft, sticky, sliceable consistency rather than a runny pool. Watch the pastry edge: the syrup bubbles at high heat and can brown the rim faster than the centre.
sourceNotes: Treacle tart appeared in British recipe collections from the late 19th century, coinciding with the introduction of Lyle's Golden Syrup in 1883. The breadcrumb thickening and lemon sharpening are standard components across household baking references (Florence White, Delia Smith, and the British WI tradition). The method here follows the standard home-baking approach.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the baked and cooled tart, well wrapped, for up to 2 months. Defrost at room temperature and warm briefly in a low oven before serving.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The tart can be baked the day before. Keep at room temperature, covered. Serve at room temperature or warm gently at 150 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 190 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 175 degrees Celsius. Middle shelf. If the pastry edge colours quickly, lay a strip of foil loosely over the rim for the last 10 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: Baking an unfilled pastry case so the crust sets before any wet filling goes in. The case is lined with baking paper and weighted with ceramic beans or dried pulses so the base stays flat and the sides do not slump.

A pastry made by rubbing cold fat into flour until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs, then binding with the minimum amount of cold water. The fat limits gluten development, giving a crumbly, tender result.

content.text: before the filling goes in, which keeps the base crisp beneath the sticky syrup. The breadcrumbs absorb the syrup as it bakes and give the filling a soft, sliceable texture rather than a liquid one. The lemon juice cuts the sweetness; without it the filling is cloying.

items.prepNote: cold; use up to 3 tbsp as needed

content.text: Put the flour, icing sugar, and cold cubed butter into a bowl. Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture looks like rough breadcrumbs and no large butter pieces remain.

Add the egg yolk and 1 tablespoon of cold water. Cut through with a knife, adding another tablespoon of water at a time until the dough just comes together. Do not overwork it. Press into a disc, wrap, and refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Lining the tin and blind baking

Preheat the oven to 190 degrees Celsius conventional. Roll the chilled pastry on a lightly floured surface to a round about 3 mm thick and large enough to line a 23 cm loose-bottomed tart tin with 1 to 2 cm overhanging.

Lift the pastry into the tin using the rolling pin. Press gently into the sides and trim the overhang. Prick the base several times with a fork. Line with a sheet of crumpled baking paper and fill with baking beans or dried pulses. Chill for 10 minutes.

Set the tin on a baking tray and blind bake for 15 minutes. Remove the paper and beans and bake for a further 5 minutes until the base looks dry and pale gold. Remove from the oven and reduce the temperature to 180 degrees Celsius.

Tip the golden syrup into a medium saucepan. To make measuring easier, sit the tin in hot water for 1 minute first: the syrup pours cleanly. Warm the syrup over low heat until it becomes runny but not bubbling. Stir in the lemon juice and then the breadcrumbs.

Pour the filling into the warm blind-baked case. Bake at 180 degrees Celsius for 20 to 25 minutes until the filling is set and barely trembling at the centre when the tin is gently shaken, and the surface has a light amber gloss. The edges will be more set than the centre.
Leave the tart to cool in the tin for 15 minutes before releasing. The filling continues to set as it cools and will be cleanly sliceable at room temperature.

attrs.heading: If something went wrong
attrs.intro: Three problems that come up with treacle tart.

items.symptom: Filling is too runny after cooling
items.cause: Underbaked, or the breadcrumb quantity was short.
items.fix: The tart needs to be barely set, not liquid, when it comes out of the oven. If it is still liquid after 25 minutes, give it another 5.
items.avoid: Avoid pulling the tart when the centre still wobbles freely.

items.symptom: Pastry base is soft and damp
items.cause: Filling went into a raw case, or the blind bake was too short.
items.fix: The base should look dry and pale gold after the uncovered bake before filling goes in.
items.avoid: Avoid skipping the 5-minute uncovered bake after removing the beans.

items.symptom: Pastry rim is very dark before the filling sets
items.cause: Oven hot spot or the rim is thinner than the base.
items.fix: Lay a strip of foil loosely over the rim after 15 minutes in the oven.
items.avoid: Avoid placing the tart on the top shelf where the rim catches direct heat.

attrs.title: Getting sticky syrup out of the tin
attrs.body: Sit the sealed tin of golden syrup in hot water for 60 seconds before opening. The syrup pours cleanly rather than slowly dribbling down the side. Weigh the tin and syrup together, tip the syrup out until the tin is 400 g lighter, then scrape the last of it out with a spatula.
